comments.author: pagetable
comments.text: Neat idea, but I'm confused about the execution model. Spreadsheets are inherently reactive dataflow graphs — when cell A1 changes, everything downstream recomputes. Compiling to Wasm implies a static compilation step. So what happens when the user edits a cell? Do you recompile the whole sheet, or just the dirty subgraph?

replies.author: mlemvik
replies.text:
OP here — good question, this was the hard part. Each strongly-connected region of the dependency graph compiles to its own Wasm function, and the runtime keeps a topological schedule of those functions. Editing a formula only recompiles the region it belongs to (usually a handful of cells), and editing a *value* recompiles nothing at all, it just re-runs the affected functions.

The win is that a column of 100k rows with the same formula shape compiles to one loop over a linear memory segment instead of 100k interpreted evaluations. On my benchmark sheet (financial model, ~400k formula cells) a full recalc went from 2.1s in my old interpreter to 60ms.

replies.author: pagetable
replies.text: That makes a lot more sense, thanks. The columnar loop trick is basically what the big engines do with shared formula records, but doing it through Wasm codegen is a nice twist. How do you handle spill ranges / dynamic arrays, where the shape of the output isn't known until runtime?

replies.author: warmstart
replies.text: 60ms for 400k cells is impressive but I'd want to see the recompile latency numbers too. If typing a new formula into a cell costs 300ms of codegen before first paint, users will perceive it as slower than the 2.1s interpreter, because the interpreter gives you the edited cell's value instantly.

replies.author: pagetable
replies.text: The architecture doc covers this — edits evaluate through a fallback interpreter immediately and the compiled version swaps in asynchronously. Tiering, basically. Codegen for a typical region is quoted at 3-8ms, so the window you're worried about exists but it's small.

comments.author: bitrotting
comments.text: Obligatory question for any spreadsheet post: how do you handle floating point? If SUM() over the same numbers gives different results depending on which compiled loop shape you picked, accountants will hunt you down. Reassociating float addition for SIMD changes the answer.

replies.author: decimaldrift
replies.text: The numerics page addresses this head-on: strict left-to-right accumulation by default, precisely so results stay bit-identical with the interpreter fallback. There's an opt-in fast-math mode per sheet that enables pairwise summation — which is actually *more* accurate on average, but not reproducible against the strict mode. Documented tradeoff, off by default. More care than I expected from a solo project.

comments.author: shredsheet
comments.text: I built something adjacent a couple years ago — a spreadsheet-to-SQL transpiler for a reporting team (writeup at shredsheet-notes.example.com). The lesson that nearly killed the project: circular references. Real-world sheets use intentional circularity with iterative calc turned on, for things like interest capitalization. How does a compile-to-Wasm model handle a cycle that's supposed to converge?

replies.author: lambdacurious
replies.text: Not OP, but this is answered in the FAQ: cycles compile to a fixpoint loop — the whole SCC becomes one function that iterates until max-delta < epsilon or an iteration cap, same semantics as iterative calc in mainstream engines. The FAQ has a wry note about the nasty part being that every engine has slightly different convergence defaults.
